summary: For ages 7-8: understand that 100 is a bundle of ten tens, just as a ten is ten ones. The core proposed experience is watching ten ten-rods fuse into one hundred-flat, mirroring the earlier ten-ones-to-one-ten move, so children are intended to experience place value as a repeating ×10 structure rather than a list of separate facts. Hold three equivalent views of 100 together (100 single cubes, 10 rods, 1 flat), and foreshadow the next rung (ten hundreds make a thousand).
misconceptions: Thinking 100 is 'ten' with zeros, not literally ten tens or a hundred ones.
Failing to see the repeating ×10 structure — treating hundreds as an unrelated new idea.
Confusing a hundred-flat with a ten-rod (not tracking which unit is which).
Believing 100 ones and 10 tens are different amounts rather than the same quantity re-unitised.
Counting the little squares one-by-one instead of trusting the unit (no unitising).

activities.title: Fuse ten tens into one hundred on an exchange bench
steps: First re-bundle ten single ones into one ten-rod as a familiar recap, naming what happened: 'ten ones make one ten'.
Gather ten ten-rods into a staging tray; as the tenth rod lands, watch the ten rods merge into a single 10×10 hundred-flat.
Say aloud the pattern that connects the two moves: 'ten of the last unit always makes one of the next'.
Use a 'three views' toggle to flip the same hundred between 100 loose cubes, 10 rods, and 1 flat, while a counter stays steady at 100.
Look at a dimmed 'next level' shelf showing ten flats waiting to become a thousand-cube, and predict what comes next.
activities.insight: 100 is literally ten tens (and a hundred ones); each new place is ten of the one before, so place value is a self-similar ×10 pattern that keeps going.

activities.title: Bundle physical materials: ten tens into one hundred
steps: Lay out ten ten-rods (or ten bundles-of-ten straws) and skip-count them: 10, 20, 30 … 100.
Physically stack or wrap all ten together and name the new unit: 'one hundred'.
State the three views in words: 100 ones, 10 tens, 1 hundred — the same quantity.
Overlay ten rods onto a 10×10 hundred-square grid to see ten rows of ten make the hundred.
activities.insight: A hundred built from real materials is the same quantity whether seen as 100 ones, 10 tens, or 1 hundred; the hundred-square bridges 'ten tens' and 'a hundred'.

activities.title: Match and complete the three views of 100
steps: Match each representation to the others: 100 ↔ 10 tens ↔ 100 ones.
Choose which option is the same amount as 100 from a set of choices.
Explain in one sentence why each view is still 100.
activities.insight: The three views of 100 are equivalent, and the ×10 pattern can be stated, not just built.

checkQuestion: Show ten tens-sticks laid out. Ask: 'If I bundle all ten of these sticks together into one block, what is that block called, and how many single ones is it altogether? How do you know?'
checkAnswer: One hundred. It is 100 ones altogether, because ten tens is 10 groups of 10, which makes 100.
